lignes.texte: When you open an incognito tab, you assume your browsing is completely invisible.
But right now, your internet provider,
your boss and Google can see every click you make. Every site you visit.
Google’s so called privacy shield is nothing more than an illusion.
Something to make you feel better while you browse. You aren’t protected… you’re
blindfolded. So what’s actually happening to your data the second you open that tab?
Turns out incognito mode was never meant
to protect your privacy… it was designed to track you.
$5 BILLION dollars.
That’s what a federal class-action lawsuit filed demanded from Google for tracking millions of
users who believed they were browsing in secret. 5 billion dollars is roughly the
GDP of Liberia. And Google, a company that earned $182 billion in revenue in 2020 alone,
decided to fight it for three and a half years before bending to the knee and settling.
Why even fight the lawsuit when they make more
than $5 billion a week in ad revenue in less than a week?
Because the lawsuit exposed something sinister.
Something far more nefarious than a software hack or data breach.
The lawsuit accused Google of doing exactly what Google was designed to do:
tracking people who used a feature that was meant to stop tracking.
What do you think happens when you open an incognito tab?
You click the little spy icon in Google Chrome, and it tells you it’s safe to browse privately. It
promises you that your history won’t be saved and your cookies will be wiped the second you close
the window. Sure, it might say your employer, or your school, might be able to track you.
But it buries the lede.
The core promise, the one the little spy-hat icon is selling, is private browsing.
And millions of Americans believe it.
What happens behind the scenes is straightforward. Chrome just deletes your
local history file when you’re done. That’s it. Your IP address, your server requests,
Google’s ad trackers and the Google Analytics code logging your visit all remained intact.
But let's be clear about what incognito mode doesn’t do. It doesn’t encrypt your
internet traffic. It doesn’t mask your location. And it doesn’t let
you opt out of tracking scripts that are running on the website you’re visiting.
Its real life function is to clear out your browser's local diary while
leaving a carbon copy at the office for safe keeping. Not your office…
Google’s.
It was this deception that triggered the Brown v. Google lawsuit. Four California residents
argued Google misrepresented the feature. It was marketed as a privacy shield while
simultaneously harvesting user data through the very tools Google sells to advertisers.
It’s a pretty big deal.
But the word “incognito” is technically defined as “having one’s
identity concealed.” It’s reasonable to assume the product would do that.
Google’s defense was corporate gaslighting. “We never told you it was private,” they claimed.
They pointed to the vague disclaimer, the one about websites and employers. They
argued that sophisticated users understood the limitations. According to Google, "private" in
"private browsing" referred to privacy from local users, not the tech giant watching you in secret.
Every time your browser loads a page, it secretly hands off a resumé of exactly who you are. Even
with incognito mode on, your cookies cleared and history wiped, your browser has to identify itself
to a web server. In a fraction of a second, it spits out an insane amount of information:
your screen resolution, browser version and operating system, timezone, language,
every font installed on your system, whether you're blocking ads and your graphics card model..
None of this is a secret. They’re just technical stats that get thrown around as part of routine
handshake data. On the surface, it’s boring, functional, even innocuous.
But when you combine them all together, something interesting happens.
The odds that any other device in the world produces that exact combination are actually
astronomically low. The Electronic Frontier Foundation tested this with their fingerprinting
tool, called Panopticlick, later renamed to Cover Your Tracks. It measured how many
browsers in their database exactly matched a given fingerprint. Across hundreds of thousands
of browsers tested, 83% were entirely unique, identifiable to a single device.
Every piece of technical data your computer pings off points directly back to you.
This whole process is called browser fingerprinting. It’s the reason Incognito
Mode is nothing more than digital decoration. You can delete every cookie in Chrome's storage.
You can open a fresh private window with a clean slate. The moment your browser
loads a page running a fingerprinting script, you’ve signed your real name.
But that’s just the beginning.
There’s a version that should really worry you.
Canvas fingerprinting is when a tracking script instructs your browser to draw an
invisible image from strings of text and gradients using HTML5’s canvas element.
Your browser draws it instantly. Because graphics rendering depends on your GPU,
your graphics driver, and your operating system's font rendering engine,
the image the computer draws is microscopically different from every other computer on Earth.
The script reads the pixel-level output and hashes it into a unique identifier. This happens in
milliseconds. You never see it. Disabling cookies has no effect. Incognito mode has no effect.
Advertisers and data brokers have known about this
since about 2012. It's one of the tools that made their fortunes.
Your hardware drew them the pictures they needed to sell
better advertisements and extract better data.
And they kept the picture for themselves.
But before Chrome has rendered a single pixel,
your device must cross a network to find the server it’s looking for.
That’s where the next problem lies.
The padlock icon in your address bar appears whenever a website's connection is encrypted.
It means the data traveling between you and the server is scrambled well enough that
nobody in the middle can read it. It’s called Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure, or HTTPS.
HTTPS protects the text you send, your bank password, medical records and the content
of your request. It’s all encrypted. HTTPS is great for stopping hackers,
but it doesn’t protect the fact that you're talking to that server in the first place.
When your browser reaches out to load a website, it has to announce the site's domain name before
the encrypted connection is established. This is a technical requirement called the Server Name
Indication, or SNI. Because the encryption hasn't started yet, the SNI field is sent in plain text.
That means your Internet Service Provider, be it Comcast, AT&T, Verizon,
or whoever is running the pipe your internet traffic flows through, can see every domain
name you visit. They can’t see the specific pages or content you see. But every site,
timestamp, frequency with which you visit, and in some cases the volume of data transferred is
visible. And in some cases, it’s enough to make educated guesses about what you were doing there.
That’s also true in incognito mode.
Your ISP is upstream from Chrome’s cookie jar. Chrome can clear whatever
it wants after your because your ISP never cared about your local file
system. It only cared about the packets of data traveling through their pipes.
ISPs can legally sell those packets in the United States.
In 2017, Congress repealed the FCC’s broadband privacy rules,
stripping away the requirement for ISPs to get your consent before sharing browsing data. The
major providers immediately promised they wouldn’t voluntarily sell their end-users’ information.
But it didn’t stop them from collecting it.
Instead they switched to a system where your ISP collects your data by default and
buries the opt-out. As of 2024, Comcast's Xfinity, for instance, was automatically
opting customers into the storage of what it classifies as sensitive personal information.
Comcast doesn't sell this data outright, but it does use it to serve personalized ads and
recommendations. If you manage to find the hidden opt out setting, you get the disclaimer:
"Even when off, we may still use your sensitive personal information for certain purposes."
It’s the exact same corporate gaslighting as Chrome. In this
environment, incognito mode becomes a closed curtain on a glass house.
Open any major news website in an incognito tab in Chrome and hit F12. Look at the network requests
firing the moment the page loads. Ignore the requests going to the news site, look at the
other ones. Before you've read a single headline, you'll find a request going to Google Analytics.
Because the code is embedded directly into the site,
Google Analytics loads automatically and pings Google's servers instantly.
The scale of this tracking is immense.
Google Analytics runs on more than half of the top 1 million websites on the internet.
It runs on news sites, recipe blogs, nonprofit homepages and even hospital patient portals.
Website owners rely on it to understand their traffic and because it’s free. Most
of them are too indifferent to care about what Google does with its data on the back end.
What Google actually does is build a behavioral profile of your life across the internet.
This is part of why incognito mode is broken as a privacy tool. You might be
trying to hide from your peers, or from the site you are visiting. But you’re
also trying to hide from Google, which is embedded in the site you're visiting.
When you close the incognito window, Chrome will wipe its cookies. But Google’s database
will still have the initial site request cross-referenced against
your fingerprint and associated with your IP address, recorded to the second.
Google Ad Manager compounds this process.
If the site displays ads, Google’s ad code immediately scans your browser,
runs the targeting logic, and selects an ad based on the automated inference of who
you are. And all of that happened inside the incognito tab, without any cookies to speak of.
The ads don’t need cookies when it has your fingerprint.
If you've been logged into any Google product in any browser tab during your session, that data
can bleed across in ways that are technically defensible under Google's terms of service.
The tracking machine processes tens of billions of impressions per day. Each impression is a
data point tied to a user identifier. Advertisers don't need to know who you are specifically. They
just need to know that you visited a certain site on a certain day so they target you with an ad.
Browser fingerprints hand it to them on a silver platter.
And you can't stop it.
Documents produced in federal litigation proved Google was aware of this deception. In 2021,
a federal judge ordered the unsealing of internal Google communications produced during discovery in
Brown v. Google. Those documents revealed the company’s own “Spy Guy” icon was misleading.
In 2019, Google's own Chief Marketing Officer, Lorraine Twohill,
wrote directly to CEO Sundar Pichai arguing the company should “make Incognito Mode
truly private”. The alternative was relying on “fuzzy, hedging language.”
Pichai was informed that calling it private ran “the risk of exacerbating known misconceptions.”
His response was to shelve the issue because he “didn't want to put incognito under the
spotlight.” Internal filings quoted employees describing the product as “a confusing mess.”
Google chose to protect its bottom line rather than its user.
They made adjustments to the splash screen wording over the years. But they didn’t change
the name or change the icon. They didn’t bother to add a disclaimer that Google’s
advertising and analytics infrastructure would continue operating inside the private window.
The data was too valuable to give up.
When they were caught, they served up classic corporate double-speak.
They claimed the fine print was accurate and that users hadn’t read it properly.
The Federal Court didn’t buy it.
In December 2023, after 3 and a half years of litigation, Google settled.
The settlement didn’t include a single cent for the hundred of millions of users Google
systematically lied to for 7 straight years. Instead, Google agreed to destroy billions
of stored data records from incognito-mode browsing activity. They were forced to block
third-party cookies in incognito by default for 5 years. And they were ordered to kill
the private-browsing detection signal they built to detect when you switched to private browsing.
To comply with the ruling, Google also updated its incognito splash screen.
It now acknowledges that websites and Google may still collect your data even
in private mode. The word “may" appears where a more accurate “will” would ordinarily live.
Google never admitted wrongdoing. The settlement changed nothing about how
incognito mode works today. The technical architecture, including the fingerprinting,
the ad network integration, and the ISP visibility remains fully operational.
If incognito mode doesn't protect you, what does?
The honest answer is there’s no single magic button. Instead,
a digital arms race is unfolding being tracking networks and privacy tools like VPNs,
specialized browsers and encrypted DNS protocols.
The fallout of this is a deeply fractured internet. Tech giants are altering browsers to
stop popular ad blockers and tracking protections. They want to make sure their data harvesting
remains unobstructed. Because the legal system moves at a crawl, companies will continue to
rely on vague wording and fine print. It’s worth the risk when the user data is worth billions of
dollars. The profits outweigh any regulatory fines or class actions that come their way.
As tracking mechanisms evolve from basic cookies to invisible digital fingerprints,
the burden of privacy is put on you, the user. The reality of the modern internet is simple…
If the site is free, the user is the product.
You thought Google built you a private window to protect you.
That window was always one way.
Google helped build the internet we browse today. But now, they're doing the opposite,
they’re actively destroying it. Watch “Google Just Killed Websites. It's Not
Good.” to see how their AI is reshaping the web.
